subject: treasureHoard
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: treasure hoard: coins, gems, chest, crown, goblets.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm planning a treasure hoard prop module with a League of Legends-style painterly aesthetic—coins, gems, a chest, crown, and goblets with glowing gold accents—and thinking through how the root joint structure needs to work since this is a static prop group rather than a creature with multiple joints.

I'm sketching out the import list for the builder utilities and style kits I'll need, and double-checking which helper functions are actually exported from the main module before relying on them.

Now I'm figuring out the chest's spatial layout: body box dimensions and center position, and whether to treat the lid as a separate hinged joint rotated backward to show an open, overflowing chest versus just placing lid parts directly in rotated model space.

Working through the right-hand rule, I confirm a negative rotation angle tips the lid's front edge upward, so I'll use roughly -110 degrees for the open position. For the lid's shape, I'm planning a half-cylinder barrel lid oriented along the X axis with capped ends, built from a cylinder geometry with a partial theta length.

The underside of the lid will be visible when open, so I should add a thin red plush lining plate there to simulate velvet, placed at the bottom of the lid geometry. I'm also working out the hinge pivot point, placing it near the back of the body so the lid rotates correctly around the arc's center.

Working out the rotation math to confirm the lid swings up and back around 105 degrees, with the curved top ending up facing down-back and the flat underside facing up-forward once open.

Now I'm thinking through the body structure: a wooden plank box with metal corner bands and a front lock plate bearing a hextech emblem, with a heaping mound of gold coins filling the interior just above the rim.

I need to keep the part budget tight, so instead of sticking hundreds of individual coin cylinders onto the pile, I'll merge groups of coins into single geometries so each cluster only costs one part while still looking like a scattered heap.

I'll merge plain coins into three parts with varied gold tones ("#f2b92c", "#ffd25a", "#c98a1c") plus a separate textured part for emblem coins, relying on the cylinder's top-cap UV mapping to show the circular drawing cleanly, though I'm aware the side UVs will stretch the texture awkwardly along the thin edge.

To avoid alpha-cutting issues on the drawn texture, I'll fill the background rectangle with solid gold before drawing the emblem, so there's no transparency to worry about. For positioning, I'll write a helper function that builds coin geometry with position and rotation applied before merging, then scatter a mound of coins using radial sampling (sqrt of random times radius) so they cluster naturally around a chosen point near the chest.

Now I'm sketching the overall scene layout from a top-down view: the chest sits centered with a spilling mound of coins in front that overlaps its front lip, and a golden crown with arches, points, and gems perched prominently on top of that mound as the visual centerpiece.

I'm placing supporting elements around this focal point — a standing goblet on a side pile, another knocked over and spilling nearby, plus a tall jeweled chalice near the chest, and clustering a few large glowing gem crystals off to the side to add sparkle and depth.

Now I'm scattering smaller cut gems in varied colors across the piles, merged by hue for efficient glow rendering, and considering a few extra touches like stacked gold ingots or a hextech crystal glow strip, while keeping the overall scope manageable.

I'm also thinking about adding a thin pearl strand draped over the pile, built as a sweep path with bead spheres merged together, and working out the chest body dimensions and hinge placement so the wood paint with vertical plank grain and dark seams lines up correctly.

Still writing wood shader and metal band logic...

Still building the band outline geometry...

I should also check the lid's extrusion axis orientation to make sure the band stays centered correctly, then add small rivet spheres merged onto the bands and a gold lock plate with a hextech emblem on the front.

For the lock plate, I'm placing a shield-shaped extrusion centered on the body front, giving it thickness along the correct axis, and layering a textured emblem plane slightly in front of it; I'll skip the hasp tongue and chains since the lid is open anyway.

Now I'm adding interior lining details — red velvet along the body rim and lid — plus small gold corner feet caps at the four bottom corners.

For textures, I'm planning a coin face with a crown/rune emblem, a hextech shield emblem with a blue gem and wings for the chest, and figuring out how to add ornamental filigree trim around the crown band — likely through repeated decals along the ring surface rather than a wraparound texture.

I'm also sketching crimson velvet band with gold scroll decals for the crown, cyan hextech rune-glow lines for the crystal base and chest runes, a zigzag/diamond band pattern for the goblet, and scattering glowing four-pointed sparkle cards across the hoard for that extra LoL shine.

Then for other elements: wood plank paint for planks, patterned velvet lining paint, and a gold bar stamp texture for ingots. Tallying up textures: coin, chest emblem, crown scroll, goblet band, sparkle, rune, ingot stamp, and gem shine decal -- eight total.

For paints I'm planning gold (custom warm-top/cool-bottom gradient with streaks and highlights), wood, red velvet, bronze, silver with a blue-tinted goblet shade, and crimson. Writing custom gold paint shader...

I'm defining the gold paint function using layered noise to blend warm bronze and bright yellow tones, brightening the top with a creamy highlight and darkening the underside with a warmer bounce-light tone. I'm weighing whether to use a built-in metal preset versus hand-painting the gold for a more stylized look, deciding to write my own gold and silver functions for variety, then moving on to designing the crown's circlet base as a tapered lathed ring.

Now I'm working out the crown's structure: a lathed shell profile for the band with distinct outer and inner wall curves, plus a layered design with a gold base rim, a crimson velvet middle band, and a gold top rim. For the crown's points, I'm planning eight alternating spikes—tall gem-topped ones and shorter ball-topped ones—extruded radially from a kite-shaped outline with a sharp peak.

I'm also designing two crossing arches over the crown's top using swept catmull curves that rise from the rim to an apex, each arch rotated 90° from the other to form the classic crisscross dome shape, with transforms placing them correctly in the crown's local coordinate space.

I'm setting up a placement helper using matrix transforms to convert local points and directions into model space, plus adding a central orb with a cross on top and band gems (ruby, sapphire, emerald) arranged in a ring around the crown.

Each gem gets a gold bezel and an octahedron shape stretched slightly for a faceted look, and I'm giving the crown a slight forward and sideways tilt so it sits askew on the coin pile.

For the goblets, I'm defining a lathe profile that sweeps the whole shape in one go—foot, stem, knot, and bowl—as a series of radius-height points along the axis.

Now I'm planning three goblets with distinct designs: a standing gold one with ruby gems on the right pile, a silver chalice with sapphire near the chest on the floor, and a tipped-over gold goblet spilling coins on the front.

For the tipped goblet, I'm setting the lathe axis at a steep tilt and generating a coin trail spilling out of its mouth using a reusable coin-scattering helper function. I'm also designing a gem cluster of five hexagonal crystal prisms with pointed tops using a lathe profile.

I'm thinking the central crystal should have a hextech cyan glow, with smaller crystals in violet and teal around it, plus scattered cut gems of multiple colors at a softer glow intensity on the floor pile — drawing on League of Legends' hextech crystal aesthetic for the color palette.

For the gold pile, I'm working out how to build trapezoid-shaped ingots using a low-segment cylinder geometry rotated and scaled to approximate a square-cross-section bar, stacking six of them in a pyramid arrangement on the left side.

Counting textures now—coin, emblem, crownScroll, gobletBand, sparkle, rune, gemCrest, maybe seven total. For extra flair I'm considering a draped pendant necklace along the chest, placing beads along a curved path from the chest rim down to the mound.

Actually, hunting for collision-free placement on the mound is taking too long, so I'll skip the necklace entirely rather than risk it clipping through geometry. I'll stick with the sparkles for decoration instead.

For the gold mound itself, I'm sinking a scaled sphere into the floor so only the flattened dome protrudes, and I'll texture it with noise-based cell patterns to fake the look of individual coin edges across the surface.

Now I'm laying out the actual mound positions and sizes across the scene — a main front pile, a smaller crown pile to the left, and another near the goblet to the right.

M4 is the chest's inner mound, sized so it stays within the chest rim's width and depth while peeking just above the opening, with the rim itself forming a visible ring around it over the red lining.

I'm thinking about adding a thin red velvet-like plane just inside the rim to simulate the lining, letting the mound rise up through it so the wood border frames the opening. But the cross-bands on top sit slightly above this lining plane, so they'd end up spanning across the opening rather than wrapping around the mound, which could look off.

To fix it, I'll keep the body bands shorter so they stop right at the body's top edge instead of wrapping over the open chest, with the front band continuing separately onto the lid. I also need to nudge the lining plane slightly above the wood top face to avoid z-fighting while keeping the gap small enough not to be noticeable.

Now I'm working out a function to scatter coins across each mound using a seeded placement so the distribution looks natural but reproducible.

Computing coin surface positions on the ellipsoid mound, orienting each coin's normal to the surface with some random tilt and spin, and occasionally letting a few stand upright on edge for variety.

Now I'm tallying totals: roughly 300 coins across the mounds and spill, each a low-poly cylinder, keeping the triangle count modest. I'm grouping them into merged batches by color variant—gold, mid, deep—plus a smaller set of textured emblem coins needing proper cap UV mapping.

I'm defining the merge logic using mergeGeometries from Three.js's BufferGeometryUtils, making sure all geometries are indexed consistently before applying transforms, and setting up the root and lid joints with their bone hierarchy and pose so the chest can open.

For the Hextech cyan glow, I'm thinking about whether to add an actual glowing gem or light-shaft card inside the chest, but deciding to keep it simple and skip that in favor of sparkle effects. I'm also confirming that parts built with an explicit bone use model-space coordinates before posing, and considering whether the lid joint should use a "hinge" role to properly constrain its rotation axis.

Now I'm checking floor contact rules carefully: mounds built as full spheres centered at y=0 would sink too far below the ground, so I need to use a hemisphere geometry (upper half only, open at the bottom) so the flat base sits exactly at floor level. I'm applying the same logic to the chest body and crystal shapes, making sure tilted crystals don't let their base disc dip noticeably below y=0.

I'm now placing goblets: the gold standing goblet sits atop the M3 coin pile with its foot sunk slightly into the pile surface, while the tipped goblet C lies on its side near the M1 pile with its axis angled so coins can spill forward, positioning its base point and checking the lowest radius point doesn't clip through the floor.

That puts the mouth near z=1.35, which pushes the whole scene's depth range too wide for a comfortable camera framing, so I should compress the overall layout — tightening the chest's z-range and pulling the goblets closer in.

I'm reworking the goblet's tilt so coins spill naturally toward the pile rather than just pointing at it, computing a base and mouth position that angles forward and plotting roughly fourteen coins along the spill arc from the mouth down toward the pile.

For the silver goblet B, I'm checking placement near the second coin pile to make sure it sits outside the pile's radius, then positioning an ingot stack off to the back-left where it won't overlap with the chest.

Now I'm placing a crystal cluster off to the right, keeping enough clearance from the chest edge and the third coin pile. I'll add a glowing gem to the chest's lock plate and scatter around a dozen sparkle effects above the treasure pile for visual flair.

I'm also thinking about adding glowing cyan rune strips to the sides of the chest body, flanking the central lock plate.

For a hextech aesthetic, I want small hexagonal cyan gems with gold bezels embedded on the front bands, blending gold and cyan to match that LoL hextech style.

Now I'm figuring out the lid interior, placing a red velvet lining with gold trim along the underside of the lid, positioning it so it sits flush when the lid is closed and avoids z-fighting since the lid rotates away in the final pose. I'm planning a gold frame around the lining using thin box strips for the trim.

I'll skip extra trim on the body since the lining already covers that visually, then build the main chest body as a wood box with painted plank details, and start defining a shield-shaped outline for the lock plate using a series of points.

Still writing lock geometry...

For the crown's scroll decals, I'm placing them on the band's outer surface using radial direction vectors tied to the crown's orientation, planning for about 8 decals around the band.

Now I'm defining the crown's geometry piece by piece using lathe profiles: a bottom gold rim, a velvet band flaring from radius 0.16 to 0.19 as it rises, and a top rim, each specified as small closed polygon outlines rotated around the vertical axis.

I also need an interior cap since the arches leave the velvet dome visible underneath—sizing a scaled hemisphere so its top sits below the apex of the arches at roughly y=0.2, keeping the crimson lining tucked properly inside.

Now I'm positioning the 8 decorative points around the top rim, alternating tall gem-topped ones and shorter pearl-topped ones at 45° intervals, and working out the tangent/radial math so each fleur shape is extruded correctly in its local plane with proper thickness.

Alternating emerald for tall gems, pearl spheres for short ones, checking that the smoothing doesn't break the sharp tip corner. For the band gems, I'm placing four larger ones at the cardinal angles (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°) with smaller ones filling the mid-angles between tall crown points.

Working out the layout: band gems align under the tall points, scroll decals go under the short points at 45° offsets, maybe adding small pearl studs around the bottom rim. I'm designing a gold collar bezel using a small radial cylinder to hold each octahedron gem, and now planning the two crown arches with curved path points rising from the base.

I'll default the bone to root everywhere via a wrapping helper, then add a gold orb with cross on top, considering whether to make it a glowing hextech-style gem to match the crown aesthetic.

Now I'm working out the crown's placement and rotation in space, defining helper functions for positioning and orienting parts, and setting up the lathe and dome geometry with appropriate axis and scaling for the crown's curved shape.

For the gem on the crown, I'm considering how to orient the octahedron shape relative to the radial direction—whether it should point outward or be flattened against the surface, and figuring out the right scale factors along each axis to get a cabochon-like appearance.

Now I'm picking flat colors for each gem type (ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz, diamond) along with a glow strength, and checking whether the glow effect applies differently depending on material type.

I'm scattering gems across the piles and chest mound—small octahedrons with randomized scale and orientation, roughly 40 total spread across the three mounds plus the chest, alongside around 14 sparkle cards. I'm also deciding how to decorate the gold goblet, placing decal bands around its bowl at a few angles.

Still writing goblet decals...

For the crystals, I'll use a six-sided lathe with a pointed hex profile, tapering to a sharp tip with creased corners.

I'm positioning a cluster of differently colored crystals—big cyan, violet, teal—each with varied leaning axes and scale, arranged around the chest area with slightly different placements and tilt angles.

Skipping facet textures for simplicity, I'll instead give each crystal two stacked color sections—a darker base lathe and a lighter top—to fake depth cheaply.

Defining crystal lathe profiles...

Writing SVG code...

I'll skip extra hinge and hasp details since the lid is already covered, and the chest has no feet, so I'm moving on to double-check overall height sizing with the lid open.

Now I'm setting up the code structure: importing Three.js utilities and the builder kit functions, defining metadata, color constants, and a helper for creating vectors, then starting to define a Mound type and list for the treasure pile geometry.

Finishing the position offset so coins sit flush on the mound surface, nudging slightly outward along the normal to avoid clipping, with edge coins tilted more to look naturally scattered.

For the mounds, I'm bucketing coins into textured versus plain variants (roughly 20% textured), varying radii between 0.042 and 0.055, and using a low-poly hemisphere geometry for the mound shape itself. I'm applying flat shading to the mound material so the painted color cells read as faceted chunks rather than smooth gradients, which should still work fine combined with per-vertex paint.

For gems, I'm writing a function that scatters octahedron-shaped gems across each pile, stretching them vertically and giving each a random orientation and color from the palette, then merging them per color group — since octahedron geometry is non-indexed, I need to keep all the gem geometries consistently non-indexed so they merge cleanly.

For the ingots, I'm computing a rotated, scaled cylinder shape to approximate a rectangular bar with tapered sides, then stacking several layers of these into a small pile with slightly offset positions per layer.

I'm planning the layered stack arrangement: three bars on the bottom row, two on the middle, one on top, with minor random yaw jitter for a natural scattered look, plus a couple of loose ingots leaning against the pile. Now I'm moving on to building the goblet geometry function.

For the decal placement, I'm working out the positions around the bowl at a fixed height along the axis, computing a perpendicular basis vector to space them evenly around the circumference.

I'm also working through the right distance to position each decal's anchor point relative to the surface so it reads as "near" the mesh without clipping through it.

Now I'm sketching crown placement logic: a position and rotation defining the crown's local frame, with helper functions to convert local offsets and directions into world space, then deciding how to combine the crown's base rotation with each gem's radial-facing orientation.

For the crown points themselves, I'm generating eight spikes around the circle, alternating tall and short heights and widths, each defined by an outline profile for extrusion. Defining crown outline points...

Placing the bezel at radius 0.186 and gem at 0.19, then positioning decal scrolls at the odd angles on the band, computing their center points, orientation, and arc size so they wrap correctly around the circle.

Then I'm defining two symmetric arch curves using swept paths of gold tubing that rise from the rim and meet at the top center, with one arch rotated 90 degrees from the other to form a crossed dome shape.

To hide where the arches intersect, I'm placing a small gold orb at the peak plus a glowing cyan octahedron gem above it as a hextech-style accent instead of a cross. Beneath the arches I'm adding a flattened hemisphere dome using velvet material, slightly overlapping the band, and setting up the crown's lathe axis and placement for a second crown instance at a different position.

Checking the math, I realize the crown sinks about 4cm into the coin pile at its current height, which actually reads nicely as "set into the coins," but I'll raise it slightly to y=0.2 for safety and make sure scattered coins don't overlap the crown band itself.

I'll also set up an exclusion zone so pile coins avoid points within 0.2 of the crown's center, and similarly keep coins clear of the goblet foot on M3 and nearby gems.
